first_impression: Gorgeous deck, real engineering. But a free OSS tool for Mac RL classes: who pays, and why now?
confusing: Slide 13 market is RL classes and clubs on MacBooks, a tiny segment, with 'later hosted version and edu licenses' as a footnote
Slide 2 pitches an NVIDIA gap, but the 40x comparison is against CPU MuJoCo, not the GPU tools the problem names
Slide 12 timeline is a build log, not a business or traction point
doubts: No users or revenue; 'first users' are the presenter's own club and hackathons
40x compares a GPU against MuJoCo on a simpler planar 2D model, so it is not apples to apples
Why would anyone doing serious RL stay on Mac when cloud NVIDIA is cheap and free Colab exists
The Mac market for robot learning looks too small to build a company on
Agents wrote most of the code, so how defensible is it
questions: Who pays, how much, and what is your first dollar?
Why now: what changed in 2026 that makes Mac robot learning a market, not a hobby?
How many students or labs have actually used it outside your club?
If Apple or MLX ships its own robot sim, what remains of MacGym?
Is this a company or a portfolio piece, and which one do you want to be?

fixes.change: Replace the vague 'later edu licenses' line with a sized market (number of RL courses and MacBook-heavy clubs/schools), one named pilot, and a price point
Add a why-now line with evidence: Apple Silicon share in student and edu hands, MLX momentum, jax-metal abandoned Jan 2026, so the gap is open now
Show any real usage: installs, GitHub stars, or 3 classmates who trained a robot, even a small number with names
Label the 40x as 2D vs 2D CPU upfront on the headline and add a one-line moat statement (kernel codegen, backend-agnostic)
Cut or shrink the git log graphic and use the space for a roadmap with a monetization step

first_impression: Finally a demo that runs. Clean deck, real recording, install in 87 s. Slightly dense by slide 10.
confusing: Slide 10 stacks 40x, 22x, 121x and a 72% bar: too many numbers for one slide late in the session
Slide 8 shows 6.16 m/s but notes say about 6 and 6.64 in the ablation; the numbers feel inconsistent
Slide 7 shows 21.5 m, slide 14 shows 21.9 m and 22.0 m: slightly different 'same run' figures
Slide 5 'brain runs on an iPhone' is a claim with no demo
doubts: Real-world ease: 87 s install was measured with a warm pip cache on the author's own machine
Planar 2D only limits what users can build; unclear how far the Python robot API goes beyond walkers and tripods
Docs and playground polish after a 4-hour build: how many rough edges are hiding
Whether a stranger on a base M1/M2 gets the same 'about a minute', since numbers are from an M3 Pro
questions: What does a first-time user hit when they try a robot that is not your examples?
Does it run on a base M1 or M2 and how long does training take there?
What is the onboarding path for a teacher running 30 students on one lab?
Which of CLI, playground, or Gymnasium wrapper do you expect people to actually use?
What breaks if I give it a bad robot definition: do I get a useful error?

fixes.change: Reduce to the 40x headline plus one bar; move the 121x decomposition and 72% PPO bar to backup so the slide reads in 5 seconds
Add benchmark times for base M1/M2 and a 'works on' line so a typical user knows what to expect
Show a 3-line first-run quickstart (install, new, train, view) with a real timing, instead of the long CLI log
Make the numbers consistent across slides and notes (6.16 vs 6.64 vs ~6; 21.5 vs 21.9 vs 22.0) or label which run each comes from
Either show a 5-second clip of the exported CoreML policy running on an iPhone or soften to 'exports to CoreML'
